article_title: Targeted Skills Instruction (TSI)
citation: Targeted Skills Instruction Evidence Rating Review. (2025). https://www.edmentum.com
title: Gradual release session structure for small-group tutoring: direct instruction, guided practice, independent work
description: Each TSI session follows "a gradual release model of direct instruction, collaborative, guided practice and independent work with tutor support." This structures each 30-45 minute tutoring session so responsibility shifts from tutor-led instruction to collaborative and guided practice and finally independent work, with the tutor available throughout. The pattern was implemented in every session of the studied program.
requirements: A tutor supporting each phase of the session
short sessions of 30-45 minutes repeated three or more times per week
target_learners: K-12 students in small tutoring groups of 2-6
target_learning_goals: reading and math skill development
examples: TSI sessions in the New Jersey study ran three 30-40 minute sessions per week following this structure
key_sources: Targeted Skills Instruction Evidence Rating Review. (2025). https://www.edmentum.com

article_title: Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2020). Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 45, issue 1.
title: Use grouped administrative data with design-based methods to improve data access for RCT analysis
description: The article recommends analyzing RCTs with grouped administrative data "to help improve data access," using design-based estimators formed as group-level averages. This allows evaluators to estimate average treatment effects when individual-level data cannot be obtained, provided the design conditions the article identifies are met.
requirements: RCT designs of the types covered: clustered and blocked designs, and models with weights and covariates
constraints: Subgroup analyses via ecological inference yield large design effects and are not covered by the tolerability result
target_learners: education researchers and evaluators conducting RCT analyses
target_learning_goals: estimating average treatment effects with restricted data access
examples: The article demonstrates the approach with empirical examples using real-world education RCT data
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2020). Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 45, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/analyzing-grouped-administrative-data-for-rcts-using-design-based-methods

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Make greater use of professional accountability in education
description: The review recommends that policymakers "make greater use of professional accountability, which has historically been underutilized in education." Professional accountability is one of the four forms in the review's taxonomy, and the authors argue its underuse represents an opportunity as states redesign accountability systems under ESSA. The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis of laboratory and field evidence on how each accountability form motivates educators.
requirements: Policymakers with discretion over accountability system design, as afforded by the Every Student Succeeds Act
target_learners: K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of educational practice
examples: The review positions professional accountability as historically underutilized relative to outcome-based high-stakes testing since NCLB.

article_title: Q&A: Grades & Test Scores
citation: Key Questions: How important are course grades as predictors of students' future success? (2025). UChicago Consortium / FutureEd. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use course grades as the primary indicator for assessing academic readiness, with standardized tests as supplementary information
description: The article recommends that when choosing a single measure for assessing academic readiness, course grades should come first because they are the most comprehensive indicator of preparation, while tests like the SAT and ACT "provide some additional information." Grades are likened to a full scouting report and tests to a sprint-time measure: useful but partial. The principle applies to admissions, advising, and readiness decisions discussed in the interview.
requirements: Grades must be interpreted knowing that grading practices differ across teachers and schools, though GPAs average out those differences.
constraints: Some studies using restricted samples or weighted or self-reported GPAs reach different conclusions, so data quality and study design matter.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students being assessed for academic readiness
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of students' general academic preparation and readiness for further academic work
examples: The interview advises that if focusing on one measure for assessing academic readiness, grades provide the most comprehensive information, with SAT/ACT scores adding some additional information.
key_sources: Key Questions: How important are course grades as predictors of students' future success? (2025). UChicago Consortium / FutureEd. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Academic Productivity of Chicago Public Elementary Schools
citation: Anthony S. Bryk, Yeow Meng Thum, John Q. Easton, Stuart Luppescu. (1998). Mining Productivity: How to Read Your Productivity Profile. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Group grade-level profiles into primary, intermediate, and upper-grade summaries so accountability promotes cooperative improvement across grade levels
description: Because adjacent-grade profiles are negatively related and single-grade judgments mislead, the guide recommends grouping two or three grades together for accountability analyses. It argues "a good accountability system should promote cooperative improvement efforts among faculty across grade levels," creating incentives for teachers to work cooperatively. Chicago elementary schools' K-8 structure supports summaries of primary (grades two to four), intermediate (five and six), and upper (seven and eight) grades.
requirements: Sufficient matched two-year data within each grade grouping to report the summary
constraints: Summary labels are based on the output trend of the final grade in the grouping and the average gain trends of the grades in the grouping
target_learners: Students in Chicago public elementary schools, kindergarten through grade eight
target_learning_goals: School-level improvement in reading and mathematics achievement
examples: The guide reports Primary Grades Summary (grades two, three, and four), Intermediate Grades Summary (grades five and six), and Upper Grades Summary (grades seven and eight) where information suffices
key_sources: Anthony S. Bryk, Yeow Meng Thum, John Q. Easton, Stuart Luppescu. (1998). Mining Productivity: How to Read Your Productivity Profile. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Achievement and Growth for English Learners
citation: Johnson, A. (2022). Achievement and growth for English Learners. (NWEA Center for School and Student Progress Working Paper). https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/08959048211049419
title: Use learning gains over time, and bilingual or home-language assessments, as key indicators of EL academic progress
description: The article argues that cross-sectional English-only achievement scores understate ELs' skills and fuel deficit framing, so "measures of learning gains should be considered the key indicator of EL academic progress in both instruction and accountability." It further recommends that "dual-language or home-language assessments should be provided in addition to English assessments" for high-stakes decisions, since home-language assessment removes language barriers and the English assessment tracks improvement as measured in English.
requirements: Assessment practices must align with accurately measuring and affirming students' skills and progress
Appropriate accommodations should be provided on monolingual English assessments to reduce bias from unnecessary linguistic complexity
constraints: Applies in contexts where all students must be assessed in English; the precise extent to which English scores underestimate individual EL achievement is unknown
target_learners: English Learners in K-12 public schools
multilingual students developing English proficiency
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of academic achievement and growth
equitable accountability and service-eligibility decisions
examples: The study disaggregated ever-EL data into always-EL and dually-identified subgroups to target services and address deficit-based narratives

article_title: Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools
citation: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234
title: Ground SEERNet research in educators' problems of practice rather than only in theory-driven questions
description: The paper argues SEERNet's contribution "could be enhanced by integrating a problem-based approach inspired by Improvement Science—that is, by collaborating with educators to identify the right problem of practice to focus on". Starting from educators' sense of what is important enables context-sensitive, precisely targeted interventions that are practically applicable and sustainable, while still using rigorous comparative testing within the platforms.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners to identify pressing problems of practice
constraints: Researchers must adapt methodologies to fit the data actually available via the platforms; Practitioners must find solutions that fit what digital learning platforms can reasonably do
target_learners: All students in schools using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Addressing the educational challenges educators consider most pressing
examples: The paper recommends using both practitioners' accounts of problems and SEERNet DLP data to uncover underlying issues and develop targeted interventions

article_title: Social Regulation of Learning
citation: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249
title: Gradually release teacher control so students can develop socially shared regulation of learning
description: The primer recommends that teachers deliberately reduce control over group dialogues, because students develop socially shared regulation of learning only when given opportunities to practice regulating without the teacher. "If a teacher does not offer a release, students will not have the opportunity to develop socially shared regulation of learning as the teacher is controlling the regulation." Development is "nonlinear and highly dynamic," so teachers should adjust the pace and intensity of interventions.
requirements: Teachers must monitor groups and intervene minimally yet impactfully, timely yet infrequently, and provide structure and support rather than expecting regulation to occur naturally
constraints: Students may need more intervention when encountering a brand new topic and less as they become familiar with one another; the process should be treated as nonlinear and highly dynamic
target_learners: K-12 students in collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: Socially shared regulation of learning
student agency and ownership of learning
examples: The primer suggests teachers pause 30 seconds and observe before intervening, and describes Dragnić-Cindrić et al.'s (2023) finding that teacher-controlled groups used less socially shared regulation
key_sources: Hampton, S., Glazer, K., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., & Fusco, J. (2025). Social Regulation of Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/249

article_title: Classroom Discourse
citation: Schank, P., Jenks, L., Barth, C., Crawford, C., Powers, K., & Fusco, J. (2025, May). Classroom Discourse. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/250
title: Establishing and reinforcing ground rules for respectful, equitable discussion
description: The primer recommends that teachers work with students to establish a shared understanding of norms for communication and engagement. Key ground rules include "listening attentively to classmates, speaking respectfully, using evidence to support claims, and taking turns to speak." Once established, norms should be consistently reinforced to become ingrained in classroom culture; some teachers hang posters of the agreed-upon norms.
requirements: Building rapport and practice with students initially takes time as expectations are laid out and students develop their skills
constraints: The primer notes that when students feel safe to share and challenge ideas without fear of ridicule, disagreements and dispute resolution become productive for learning
target_learners: K-12 STEM students
target_learning_goals: participation in productive, accountable classroom discussion
examples: Some teachers hang posters in their classrooms of the agreed-upon norms

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Ground personalized learning in learning sciences research on learner variability
description: The article argues that because personalization can only be as good as what is known about learners, the education community must leverage research on how students learn to "improve the accuracy and precision of personalization." It criticizes emerging definitions of personalized learning for omitting "the explicit acknowledgement of the importance of learning sciences research" and calls for translational research determining which approaches work for which students in what context. Technology should make this research accessible and usable at scale.
requirements: Access to research on learner variability; translational research on which approaches work for which students in which contexts
constraints: Not all personalization approaches, materials, and products are effective with all students in every situation
target_learners: All learners, including the growing diversity of U.S. public school students
target_learning_goals: Effective, equitable personalization of objectives, approaches, content, pace, and tools
examples: The article cites the Cooney Center/New America market scan showing most popular literacy apps reference no research, and proposes technology tools such as the Research Map to make research accessible

citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Ground breakthrough solution development in existing theory or evidence
description: Breakthrough R&D teams should leverage existing basic and applied research — the note cites the science of reading, self-determination theory, and formative assessment — to guide development. target_learning_goals: designing breakthrough solutions grounded in learning science

citation: A Toolkit to Support Evidence-Based Writing Instruction in Grades 2 Through 4 (Historical). (2025). What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Ground professional development in an evidence-based practice guide and adapt it with practitioners

Practitioner input from teachers, school leaders, or PD coaches

article_title: A level playing field: College readiness standards
citation: Michael Dahlin and Beth Tarasawa. (2013). A Level Playing Field? How College Readiness Standards Change the Accountability Game. Northwest Evaluation Association. https://www.nwea.org
title: Hold schools accountable for student growth rates rather than status measures such as proficiency or college readiness rates
description: This principle holds that because status measures largely reflect socioeconomic composition, school accountability should rest on how much students grow. The report argues status metrics are "largely controlled by socioeconomic factors beyond school control" and that growth-based policies put every student's progress into play, making them a better measure of school effectiveness than NCLB's proficiency-driven approach. The study's equivalence of growth across poverty levels provides its evidentiary basis.
requirements: A longitudinal growth measure on an equal-interval scale so student progress can be tracked over time
constraints: The report states growth models are a necessary but insufficient measure of achievement in terms of equity, since existing achievement gaps persist when students enter school
target_learners: elementary and middle school students
high-achieving students
target_learning_goals: academic growth in mathematics and reading
college readiness
examples: The study used NWEA MAP assessments, a computerized adaptive test with an equal-interval cross-grade Rasch scale, to measure growth of top-10% students over three years in high- and low-poverty schools.

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Gradual release of responsibility four-phase tutoring sequence
description: Air Tutors structures tutoring within the gradual release of responsibility (GRR) framework, a sequence of learning activities that shifts responsibility for learning from tutor to student across four phases: focused instruction ("I do it"), guided instruction ("We do it"), collaborative learning ("You do it together"), and independent learning ("You do it alone"). Tutors model cognitive processes so learners can understand metacognition and eventually replicate strategies independently. The framework need not be linear: educators may begin in any phase, and students move back and forth between components as they master skills.
requirements: Tutors introduced to the GRR framework during professional learning sessions before applying it in tutoring
constraints: The article notes the process can flow quickly or skip phases depending on the topic and student, and the framework does not have to be linear
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students in small-group math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Building student independence and confidence as independent learners and thinkers in mathematics
examples: Air Tutors tutors apply the four GRR phases within 45-minute tutoring sessions, with the goal of equipping students to move forward as independent learners rather than remaining dependent on a tutor
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673538

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase I)
citation: Bland, J. & Smith, K. (2023, February). Recruitment and retention: Pilot solutions designed by teachers of color (Phase I). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/168
title: Grow-Your-Own credential pathway for classified staff
description: One LEA implemented a Grow-Your-Own program "structured to set up pathways for classified staff to earn credentials—in part because classified staff in the LEA are, on the whole, more diverse than classroom teachers." It focuses on teacher assistants who already hold college degrees, partnering with four higher education institutions and the state teacher's union to offer varied transition-to-teaching licensure programs. The administrator estimated the LEA currently has 15 to 20 classified staff members working toward earning their teaching license, who will "serve as a pool of individuals to feed into our teacher pipeline down the road."
requirements: Partnerships with higher education institutions offering transition-to-teaching licensure programs that fit participants' learning and work-life balance
target_learners: Classified staff and teacher assistants with college degrees seeking teaching licensure
target_learning_goals: Earning teaching credentials and entering the local teacher pipeline
examples: The initiative is already in progress, with 15 to 20 classified staff members working toward licensure

The questions are organized into seven categories: early intervention services; preschool; special education; trauma/assessment; placement; school factors, strategies, and outcomes; and system issues.

school success and academic outcomes
effective data collection and sharing across education, child welfare, mental health, and judicial systems

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Grow Your Own Illinois program
description: A state-funded program that provides "scholarships and assistance for community members to become certified teachers and work in schools in the state." article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Grade the discipline, not the artefact: assess what the agent cannot satisfy
description: Because the delivered artefact in an agentic course is co-produced with an agent, the article's assessment principle is that "the grading scheme grades the discipline rather than the lines of code." Criteria are chosen so the agent cannot satisfy them in itself: framing, specification, context engineering, verification design, code review against a structured standard, multi-agent coordination, and security and governance analysis. Three commitments follow: the audit trail is gradable, the spiral is gradable as a rhythm across turns, and verification is gradable as a deliverable, with Hassan and colleagues' MRP framework as the final-deliverable standard.
requirements: Students must submit chat transcripts, commit history, context files, lessons-learned notes and verification records alongside the artefact; without these the artefact is opaque and cannot be assessed
constraints: Audit trails that are absent, opaque or evidently retrofitted score zero on process traceability regardless of artefact quality; an artefact satisfying four of five MRP criteria is treated as not merge-ready
target_learners: undergraduate students in agentic software engineering courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating framing, specification, verification design and review judgment co-producing work with an agent
examples: A student taking three turns to converge with a clear audit trail scores higher than one reaching a similar end state in one turn with no record of the reasoning; weighting is 50 per cent continuous coursework, 40 per cent project, 10 per cent closing artefact
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education
citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484

description: The system implements Retrieval-Augmented Generation via the GraphRAG framework, in which textbook material is represented as a knowledge graph to provide contextually relevant information to the Tutor Agent and course-generation pipeline. The authors chose GraphRAG over normal vector RAG on the argument that its graph structure better represents educational content relations for contextual tutoring. The Tutor Agent retrieves textbook data to ground its responses, and the course pipeline accesses GraphRAG data when constructing structured learning plans.

constraints: The article notes future work will explore the potential of different RAG architectures
target_learners: mathematics students using the tutoring platform
target_learning_goals: grounding tutor responses and generated courses in course textbook content
examples: The Tutor Agent retrieves textbook data to ground its responses during guided tutoring interactions

article_title: The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions
citation: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143
title: Graduated assessment rubric separating answer correctness from method validity
description: The rubric adapts the mathematical assessment distinction between the answer mark (correct output) and the method mark (valid reasoning) to automated diagnosis. For correct-answer cases it distinguishes four categories: clear reasoning, needs clarification, misconception detected, and wrong answer. The paper argues a binary formulation "collapses Options 2 and 3, either falsely accusing students whose explanations are merely brief, or losing the routing signal that distinguishes unclear from flawed reasoning." It grounds the design in Black and Wiliam's formative assessment steps.
requirements: Requires student responses containing a short written explanation alongside the answer, plus a mark scheme describing the expected reasoning method
constraints: Short explanations (average 16 words) can be genuinely ambiguous, so the rubric treats diagnostic ambiguity as a property of the evidence rather than a failure of the model
target_learners: school mathematics students on the Eedi platform
target_learning_goals: detecting hidden mathematical misconceptions in student reasoning
examples: The paper evaluates the rubric with BERT-base, Gemini 3 Flash, and Gemma 4 26B on 3,702 held-out Eedi responses
key_sources: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: Greedy student-to-project assignment algorithm with dynamic skill weighting and tunable preference weight
description: The matching system iteratively computes a match score for every student-project pair, combining a student's preference score weighted by an instructor-tunable parameter α with skill self-ratings weighted by a dynamic skill weight β. As the article explains, "as the algorithm progresses, and more students are assigned to the project, the value ofβp(k)for unfulfilled skills will increase leading to a higher match score for students that satisfy those skills." A skill counts as unfulfilled when no assigned student self-rated proficiency of 3 or higher on the survey's 1–5 scale. The greedy process selects the highest match score each round, with ties broken by preference then randomly, and projects with higher average preference receive more capacity up to a fixed team-size limit of five.
requirements: Instructor-defined preference weight α
Student skill and preference survey data
A predetermined skill list shared by surveys and LLM extraction
constraints: The current method can favor projects with many required skills at the expense of those with rare but critical skills
All skills are currently treated equally, with fulfillment based on a single student's intermediate-level rating
target_learners: senior-level computer science capstone students
target_learning_goals: balanced teams with skill coverage and preference alignment
examples: Used to form teams in UC Merced capstone courses with team sizes of three to five students
key_sources: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572

article_title: Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction
citation: Davor I (2026) Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction. Front. Educ. 11:1869961. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1869961
title: Geometry Reasoning and Proof Test (GRPT) with perception and attitude questionnaire
description: The study used two instruments: the Geometry Reasoning and Proof Test (GRPT), combining multiple-choice and open-ended items measuring students' capacity to interpret geometric representations, justify mathematical statements, and develop logical proofs; and a five-point Likert perception and attitude questionnaire with two conceptually distinct dimensions covering usefulness, clarity, guidance, and instructional support, and enjoyment, confidence, satisfaction, and willingness to engage. The GRPT "yielded a Spearman-Brown split-half reliability coefficient of 0.859", and the questionnaire subscales showed Cronbach's alphas of 0.878 and 0.914.
requirements: Items were adopted from the geometry assessment literature and piloted with 30 students from a different school before use.
constraints: Perceptions and attitudes were assessed only among participants in the experimental group.
target_learners: senior high school students in geometry courses
target_learning_goals: geometric reasoning
proof construction

article_title: Emotion Regulation and Academic Burnout Among Youth: a Quantitative Meta-analysis
citation: Ioana Alexandra Iuga · Oana Alexandra David. (2024). Emotion Regulation and Academic Burnout Among Youth: a Quantitative Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09930-w
title: Gross's process model of emotion regulation as the explanatory framework linking ER strategies to academic burnout
description: The article adopts Gross's process model of emotion regulation, which "lays out the sequential actions people take to regulate their emotions during the emotion-generative process": situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. It uses this model to explain how students' ER strategies, as adaptive or maladaptive reactions to academic stressors, shape their susceptibility to school burnout. The article also distinguishes ER abilities from ER strategies as interconnected approaches.

constraints: The article states the included studies are predominantly cross-sectional, so the model's causal directionality from ER to burnout cannot be established from this evidence

target_learning_goals: managing academic stress and emotions to protect academic well-being and reduce burnout

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Groundedness continuum of external representations: grounded versus idealized manipulatives
description: Belenky and Schalk's framework, as discussed in the commentary, views manipulatives as a particular form of external representation arranged along a groundedness continuum. As the commentary puts it, "On one end of the continuum are grounded representations that share the visual appearances of objects they represent (e.g., pizzas to represent fractions) while on the other end are idealized representations with superficial characteristics stripped away". The framework organizes predictions about learning, transfer, and interest, with idealized representations expected to facilitate transfer more than grounded ones.
requirements: Classification of a manipulative's position on the groundedness continuum to generate predictions about learning and transfer
constraints: Related research is inconsistent: some studies suggest grounded manipulatives may inhibit learning relative to idealized representations (Kaminski et al. 2009; McNeil and Jarvin 2007)
target_learners: Classroom learners, particularly children in mathematics instruction
target_learning_goals: Learning, transfer, and interest outcomes from manipulative-based instruction
examples: Pizzas representing fractions as grounded representations; plastic circles representing fractions as idealized representations

Its emphasis is on "a gradual transfer of control over student learning processes from the teacher and/or other instructional agents to students." The review argues successful change requires addressing all learning components, not just strategies.

Diagnosis of students' own way of learning and preconceptions, as in Vermunt (1995)

self-regulation of learning
meaning- and application-directed learning patterns

article_title: Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement
citation: Prast, E. J., Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Luit, J. E. H. (2018). title: GROW teacher professional development programme for differentiated mathematics instruction
description: The GROW PD programme is a multi-component, year-long professional development intervention designed following characteristics of effective teacher PD from the literature. It consisted of three main components: PD for all teachers (ten three-hour team meetings across the schoolyear, six led by educational consultants and four by school-based project coaches, using interactive lectures, practical exercises, and adapted Lesson Study), additional training for internal project coaches (five regional meetings, coaching and lesson-observation duties, follow-up and train-the-trainer packages), and active involvement of the principal (intake meetings, intervision meetings, a school-level implementation plan). article_title: A preliminary report of some group tests of general intelligence.
citation: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Use group tests as an impersonal first-stage screener to sort out subnormal children for individual Binet testing
description: The article recommends group tests as an impersonal method for locating children of doubtful mentality, because teachers' estimates are unreliable: teachers judge a sweet, docile child bright and overlook age. As the author states, "The use of the group tests in the survey has been to sort out the subnormal children, or those whose mentality is questionable, for further individual testing." Classification by number of tests passed approximates the intelligence quotient for borderline children.
requirements: If more complete standardization of the tests confirms the present results, grade- and age-normed numbers of tests passed must be available for comparison

title: Greene's tentative analysis of language ability into oral and written expression with mechanical, grammatical and rhetorical factors
description: The article presents a tentative analysis dividing language ability into oral expression (voice, articulation, grammatical errors, vocabulary, audience attitudes, logical organization) and written expression. citation: Greene, H. A. (1928). Tests for the Measurement of Certain Phases of Linguistic Organization in Sentences. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Organization Test: sentence-rearrangement exercises measuring organization ability within the sentence
description: The Organization Test confronts the subject with a limited number of ideas presented in jumbled order which, when properly arranged, make a complete logical statement. Sentences from lower grade readers and primers were divided into thought units, jumbled by randomized number permutations, and answered by writing the numbers in the proper order rather than rewriting the sentence. Two parallel forms of ten exercises each were standardized, with a total possible score of 100 points per form.

citation: H. O. R. (1922). Another Manual on the Technique of Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Books preparing teachers for school subjects should be grounded in scientific analyses of learning in those subjects rather than in empirical, a-priori pedagogy
description: The reviewer holds that teacher-education books should build on the scientific method of attacking educational problems and on measurement-based analyses of learning in each school subject. He faults Davis' Technique of Teaching because its bibliographies refer prospective teachers to "other books in the same category as his own—empirical and a -priori pedagogies" rather than to such analyses.

title: Group intelligence tests arose because individual Binet-scale examination was impractical for school-wide testing and was intensified by wartime Army testing
description: The article organizes the emerging field of group intelligence testing as a historical development: the Binet Scale and its revisions "demand the individual examination of the child", which made routine school testing impractical, and demand for group tests was "greatly intensified by our sudden entry into the World War". The wholesale testing of recruits stimulated publication of many tests, creating "great need for comparison, analysis and evaluation".

article_title: The relation of class standing to college tests.
citation: Sunne, Dagny. (1917). The Relation of Class Standing to College Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(4), 193-211.
title: Use group testing of college students as a feasible, time-saving measurement approach, with repeated trials and both quantitative and qualitative scoring for memory tests
description: The article concludes that group administration of standardized tests is practical and efficient for college students. It states "Group testing of college students is feasible and an economy of time especially in measuring speed and accuracy of association and memory", and recommends at least two trials of association and memory tests and both quantitative and qualitative scoring of memory results.
requirements: Standardized time limits and adapted group instructions, as the article notes individual and group method differences affect results
constraints: Some tests proved too easy for the majority and may become mainly tests of writing speed if the time limit is shortened; the Ink Blot test was least suited to group work

article_title: Mentality tests: A symposium.
citation: Hollingworth, H. L. (1917). Mentality Tests: A Symposium. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mentality+Tests%3A+A+Symposium%22+Hollingworth
title: Standardize individual tasks on graded bases and build graded series of single-process tests before combining them into composite scales
description: This principle orders test-development work from the bottom up: particular tasks and tests are first standardized on graded bases, and graded series of tests of a single, definite, objectively describable process are built. Hollingworth states his interest is "in seeing particular tasks and tests standardized on some graded basis, such as age, school grades or standing, occupational success." Only once many such single tasks exist, in duplicate or triplicate sets, may testers "combine them as we like into sectioned or universal scales," correlate them with other characteristics, and classify the scales by the mental functions they involve.
requirements: A considerable number of single tasks must first be standardized on a graded basis such as age, school grades or standing, or occupational success, and be available in duplicate or triplicate sets.
target_learners: individuals of different ages, school grades, and occupations assessed with mental tests
target_learning_goals: objective description and grading of specific mental processes such as language ability, musical ability, and reading
examples: Hollingworth cites Roemer's study of association reactions, Sylvester's study of the form board, tests of musical ability, Trabue's scales for language ability, Pintner's work with the Knox cube, and Thorndike's reading scales as work of this character.

article_title: Terman vocabulary as a group test.
citation: Weeks, A. L. (1919). Terman Vocabulary as a Group Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Use the Terman vocabulary test as a written group test in secondary schools to select extreme cases early in the school year
description: The article recommends administering the Terman vocabulary list to whole classes in written form rather than individually, because group and oral results agree closely. The author states the correlation is "sufficient to warrant the use of the group method of vocabulary testing in secondary schools. By this means, extreme cases can be selected early in the school year." This makes an individual-format measure practical for whole-class screening.

A second, alternate word series reserved for the subsequent individual test so no word repeats across formats

elementary pupils above the fifth grade
target_learning_goals: vocabulary knowledge assessment
screening to identify extreme cases early in the school year

article_title: Individual differences in grammar grade children. A comparative study of forty-four seventh and eighth grade pupils.
citation: Chambers, W. G. (1909). Individual Differences in Grammar Grade Children: A Comparative Study of Forty-Four Seventh and Eight Grade Pupils. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Grade rigid grading and promotion on natural rather than artificial distinctions, since a rigid system works injustice to individuals
description: The article argues that because pupils of a given grade are not equally endowed in any one subject and no pupil holds the same rank across studies, "a rigid system of grading and promotion must work injustice to individuals." Since grading is nonetheless necessary, it "should be made to depend on natural, rather than artificial, distinctions." This challenges the assumption that all members of a class should proceed at the same pace in all subjects.

constraints: The article accepts that grading remains necessary under present conditions and does not propose abolishing it

target_learning_goals: fair and accurate placement and promotion of pupils according to their actual abilities
examples: Rank analysis of 44 pupils showed the least variation of ability in any pupil was five different ranks in ten different traits; the poorest eighth-grade addition and spelling records were surpassed by a randomly selected third-grade child.

article_title: Mentality tests for college freshmen.
citation: Uhl, W. L. (1916). Mentality tests for college freshmen. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Group-administered timed mental tests with standard time for all are workable for securing freshman norms, with completion and opposites tests preferable to the information test

Monitors are needed to prevent overtime work, and the medians from Tables I-III may be considered norms. The completion and opposites tests are better adapted to such use than the information test.

Results support distributed test periods for group work, though individual testing may be more reliable

Distributed periods of testing on several different days in several different forms were suggested to reveal special strengths or weaknesses

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html

Each item must have only one correct answer
Answers should be placeable in a single column for scoring-form scoring

article_title: Two Important Points with Regard to Age-Grade Tables.

article_title: Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components
citation: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Group Leader Tutor: an ITS component that monitors and teaches collaborative skills in networked Jigsaw teams
description: The Group Leader (GL) Tutor was the software heart of the Intelligent Collaborative Learning System (ICLS), a client-server system on an Ethernet LAN using a shared FoxPro database. The authors state that 'The GL Tutor, a software process and the key contribution of our research, monitored and taught the effective use of collaborative skills.' It traced discussions through a finite state machine, compared used skills against optimal skills in the Collaborative Skills Network, assessed mastery by comparing successful uses to missed uses, and generated tutoring feedback based on previously stored feedback in a historical database.

title: Use graduated-prompt tutoring feedback in digital learning environments to help children with low initial ability learn analogy solving
description: The article concludes that interactive tutoring feedback implemented with graduated prompting techniques is the advisable form of feedback for advancing children's analogical reasoning, and that the strategy profiles identify which children have little understanding of the task at pretest. citation: Ronimus, M., Eklund, K., Pesu, L., & Lyytinen, H. (2019). Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 639–663. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09658-3

citation: Verena Rufai, Dominik Thüsbj, Sarah Malonecj, Stefan Küchemanndi, Sebastian Becker-Genschowe, Markus Vogelf, Roland Brünkengj, Jochen Kuhnhi. (2024). A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

description: The review frames graphing as an active generative process located at the high end of Chi and Wylie's Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive (ICAP) framework. The review uses this framing, together with generative learning theory, to predict positive effects of graphing on learning.

constraints: The review notes that the way graphing is conducted, such as manually or via tools, might also influence the learning outcome.

description: The review maps how graphing was typically implemented across the included studies. description: The article argues that memorization of rules should not form the basis of language instruction; rules should be taught through texts and examples, and for agglutinative languages like Turkish students must perceive rather than memorize suffix functions. It concludes that "Teaching grammar with texts containing information related students' own lives can lead to success", and that teachers should know their students well and build teaching on students' knowledge.
requirements: Teachers must know their students well; the article suggests establishing a database of student information such as age, country, physical properties, likes and dislikes
constraints: Preparing individualized texts or exams brings an additional workload to teachers and may not be preferred by them; the article limits its success claim to small classes
target_learners: foreign learners of Turkish
students in small grammar classes
target_learning_goals: grammatical competence in a second language
internalizing the ability to use the language properly and effectively
examples: The experimental group's examples and exams used each student's own country, siblings' names, physical appearance and place of residence with case and possessive suffixes

article_title: The Effect of Differentiated Science Curriculum on Students' Motivational Regulations
citation: Neşe Kutlu Abu, Murat Gökdere. (2018). The Effect of Differentiated Science Curriculum on Students' Motivational Regulations. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(3): 455-465. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.060312
title: The Grid Model as a differentiated curriculum framework based on depth and complexity
description: The Grid Model is a differentiated curriculum model that restructures the existing general education curriculum according to the principles of depth and complexity without changing its scope. Learning objectives, content, process and products are organized by themes, and eleven indicators are defined: "discipline's language, details, patterns, trends, unanswered questions, rules, ethics, great ideas, timing, perspective, and interdisciplinary". In this study it was operationalized as a 7-week, 42-hour differentiated Light and Sound science unit integrating disciplines such as archeology, astronomy, chemistry and design, implemented in GATE-style settings with gifted and non-gifted 4th graders.
requirements: Teachers must be trained in the model and in depth and complexity practices before implementation; pilot schemes identified problems that required additional teacher education
constraints: The article reports that teachers found it difficult to transfer knowledge of the model to classroom implementations and to evaluate student outcomes and give feedback
target_learners: 4th grade primary school students, gifted and non-gifted
target_learning_goals: Science content learning (Light and Sound unit)
motivation for self-regulation
interdisciplinary and in-depth thinking skills
examples: The study classified Light and Sound learning outcomes by Bloom taxonomy, linked them to a changing theme, and offered students choice among self-directed in-depth activities

title: Grid-based differentiated science unit pattern: thematic interdisciplinary activities with student choice
description: A unit-level instructional pattern in which a standard science unit's outcomes are reclassified by concept, principle and generalization, linked to a theme, and rewritten toward the upper levels of Bloom taxonomy. Activities are integrated across disciplines, expanded with current topics such as radio, optical and mirrored telescopes, and offered as choices so students learn in depth with self-directed topics. The article reports that "Students were offered the opportunity to choose one or several of the activities developed for them to learn in depth with self -directed topics independently", with posters at an interest corner and forms for problem solving and research design.
requirements: Teacher training on the Grid model and activity implementations prior to implementation
use of a Total Talent Portfolio to gather information about gifted students for differentiation
constraints: Implementation stayed within MoNE's specified time period for the Light and Sound unit (7 weeks, 42 teaching hours)
target_learners: 4th grade primary school students in mixed-ability classes containing at least one gifted student
target_learning_goals: in-depth thinking skills
research and problem-solving skills
interdisciplinary connections in science
examples: Predictive-observation-research activities were carried out, and resource-room activities were provided for gifted students in a support classroom and university laboratory

article_title: To Give Control to Learners or Not? A Comparative Study of Two Ways of Teaching Listening
citation: Yushan Wang. (2010). To Give Control to Learners or Not? A Comparative Study of Two Ways of Teaching Listening. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 2. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Give learners more control over listening practice to foster autonomy while retaining teacher guidance
description: The article recommends that teachers follow the trend from teacher-centered to learner-centered regimes by giving students more control of learning pace, material and environment, using learners' expectations to foster autonomy, while keeping teacher lectures, assigned tasks and checks in place. It reports that students under the zero class hour model made similar achievement gains and spent more weekly time practicing, suggesting "they have become more autonomous than they were under the traditional way of listening teaching".
requirements: Teacher still provides learning aims, assignments, methods and checks via questions, quizzes and tests
Students should not be given all control; some teacher support remains
constraints: Findings come from a two-month quasi-experiment in two classes at one university with non-random subjects, so generalizability is limited
target_learners: non-English major university EFL learners
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
learner autonomy
examples: The experimental group received weekly skill lectures plus compulsory and optional out-of-class listening tasks, chose when, where, how and what to listen to, and reported practice time in weekly diaries

article_title: The Effect of Learning Styles on Academic Achievement in Different Forms of Teaching
citation: Cimermanová, I. (2018). The Effect of Learning Styles on Academic Achievement in Different Forms of Teaching. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 219-232. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11316a
title: Grasha-Riechmann social-interaction learning style model
description: The Grasha-Riechmann model classifies learners by their preferred social interaction in learning, which the article says "reflects the learners' abilities and preference to work independently, preferences to cooperate or to compete". Its classification rests on three dichotomous pairs: competitive-collaborative, avoidant-participant, and dependent-independent. The study operationalised it with the 60-item GRSLSS inventory on a five-point rating scale to profile students before the online vs in-class intervention.
requirements: A validated self-report instrument (GRSLSS, 60 items, 10 per category, five-point scale) administered before intervention
constraints: Grasha (2002) is cited as saying style preferences "can and often does change depending upon how the teacher structures the class"
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: identifying learner social-interaction preferences to plan teaching formats
examples: The inventory was filled in by all 81 participants at the beginning of the semester before the quasi-experiment began.

article_title: Grammar for Writing: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Torgerson, D., Torgerson, C., Mitchell, N., Buckley, H., Ainsworth, H., Heaps, C., & Jefferson, L. (2014). Grammar for Writing: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation
title: Grammar for Writing intervention (15 contextualised grammar sessions for Year 6)
description: Grammar for Writing is a literacy curriculum intervention aiming to improve the writing of Year 6 pupils through contextualised grammar teaching. It "encourages pupils to improve how their writing communicates with the reader by making connections between a linguistic feature and the effect it has on writing, rather than by focusing on grammatical inaccuracies." In this trial it comprised 15 sequential guided writing sessions delivered over four weeks, with teachers receiving three days of training, and was tested as both a universal and targeted intervention at an estimated cost of £20 per pupil.
requirements: Teachers in intervention classes received three days of training in the Grammar for Writing approach
Delivery used literacy class time with the developer-designed sequential guided writing sessions
constraints: The report concludes the evidence is insufficient to recommend widespread adoption among Year 6 pupils
Fidelity of small group delivery could not be verified in all schools as there was no fidelity assessment of adherence to the trial design
target_learners: Year 6 pupils predicted to achieve between Level 3c and Level 4b in Key Stage 2 English
target_learning_goals: Improve writing skills through contextualised grammar teaching
examples: 53 primary schools from four regions of England delivered the intervention in June/July 2013, with intervention teachers rated as delivering it with good fidelity on a 0-9 fidelity measure covering grammar terms, linking grammar effects, and talk about choices and effects

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics
citation: Anastasia Sofroniou and Konstantinos Poutos. (2016). Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics. Educ. Sci. 2016, 6, 30. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci6030030
title: Use group work in higher-education mathematics tutorials to improve performance and learning experience, with the educator actively facilitating
description: Based on its positive qualitative and quantitative findings, the article endorses adopting group work in university mathematics, particularly for topics students find challenging such as integration. It stresses that the educator plays a vital role, acting "both as an academic expert and as a classroom manager", providing guidance, balancing too much or too little assistance, and intervening facilitatively so groups complete their tasks.
requirements: Educator specifies objectives, makes instructional decisions, clarifies tasks, observes interaction, gives hints and manages the level of assistance
constraints: The article cautions that group work is not necessarily the answer to all pedagogical failings; barriers include time management concerns, assessment issues and the impact of the educator's experience and own knowledge
The study's small sample size limits generalisation, and the authors invite larger classes and longer interventions
target_learners: first-year university engineering students
target_learning_goals: improve performance on challenging mathematics topics
develop critical thinking, analytical and communication skills
examples: The article's intervention delivered only the Integration topic as group work during tutorial time over four weeks, while the rest of the syllabus continued under normal arrangements, and exam results favoured the group-work class.

article_title: The Effect of a Group Approach on the Performance of High School Mathematics Learners
citation: Dhlamini, J., & Mogari, D. (2013). The effect of a group approach on the performance of high school mathematics learners. Pythagoras, 34(2), Art. #198. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v34i2.198
title: Group approach pattern: mixed-ability groups with assigned roles, social norms, and worked-out example worksheets
description: The article's instructional pattern arranged learners in groups of five to seven representing different achievement levels, appointed a leader, an explainer and a recorder in each group, and established social norms of explaining, challenging, critiquing and supporting fellow members' solutions. Worked-out example worksheets presenting step-by-step solution guidelines "served as springboards to group discussions", after which learners attempted new tasks independently, seeking group help only when challenged. The teacher circulated amongst groups to monitor engagement and adherence to roles.
requirements: Identical worksheet tasks across conditions; teacher circulation amongst groups; assigned roles and social norms for discussion, argumentation and reflection
constraints: The article acknowledges that the group approach and the worked-out examples approach were confounded in this implementation and should be demarcated in future research
target_learners: low-performing Grade 10 mathematics learners in township high schools
target_learning_goals: problem-solving performance in Grade 10 financial mathematics
examples: In experimental schools the first author implemented the pattern for two weeks in five schools while control schools used the same worksheets under conventional teacher-led instruction

article_title: CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity
citation: Sajad Shafiee, Mansour Koosha & Akbar Afghari. (2015). CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity. English Language Teaching, 8(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p170
title: Grenfell and Harris's six-step model of strategy instruction
description: The article implements Grenfell and Harris's (1999) model of strategy instruction as the pedagogical framework for teaching prewriting strategies in all three experimental conditions. The model proceeds through an ordered sequence of steps: "awareness raising, modeling, general practice, action planning, focused practice, and evaluation". It was delivered in class for the conventional group, online for the web-based group, and both in class and online for the hybrid group, over five sessions with one strategy per session.
requirements: Delivery across five sessions, with each prewriting strategy taught and practiced in one session
constraints: In this study the model was applied only to the planning phase of writing, teaching freewriting, brainstorming, listing, clustering, and wh-questions
target_learners: Iranian EFL university sophomores in an Advanced Writing Course
target_learning_goals: Generating ideas during the planning stage of writing
Increasing writing quantity
examples: The three experimental groups experienced the model's six steps respectively over five sessions, with materials available online at the researchers' weblog for the web-based and hybrid groups

article_title: The Effectiveness of Using Group Story-Mapping Strategy to Improve Reading Comprehension of Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Nada Alturki. (2017). The effectiveness of using group story-mapping strategy to improve reading comprehension of students with learning disabilities. Educational Research and Reviews. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR
title: Group Story-Mapping Strategy with five narrative story areas
description: Group story-mapping is a graphic-organizer strategy in which students record a narrative story in five main areas: setting, characters, problem, solution, and opinion. The article describes it as a tool that "utilizes a graphic organizer to support learners to recognize the story components" and that can help students visualize connections between ideas. In this study the researcher displayed the elements on a poster, explained each component, discussed instances of each, and had participants complete story maps independently after reading a nonfiction story.
requirements: A text or story with an apparent chronological order so learners can identify characters, problem, and solution without confusion
Explicit teaching of each story-map component with guided practice before independent completion
constraints: The study implemented it with sixth-grade ESL students with specific learning disabilities in a special education classroom with a one-to-four educator-to-student ratio
target_learners: Sixth-grade ESL students with specific learning disabilities in reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of narrative text, including identifying setting, characters, problem, solution, and opinion
examples: The researcher taught the five story-map elements on a poster, then participants read the story A Hero's Name aloud and completed their story maps independently before taking the comprehension test

title: GraspLearn: a graspable multimedia system unifying digital multimedia with physical artefacts
description: GraspLearn is a CD-ROM based standalone multimedia system for ESL learning in which "GraspLearn was made up of two worlds, physical and virtual arenas." The physical arena holds RFID tags and reader, slider, spatial, force and touch sensors, five physical artefacts, a display table and peripherals; the virtual arena contains corresponding virtual learning artefacts. Learners grasp RFID-embedded physical artefacts to trigger virtual content, and answer quizzes by identifying the correct physical artefact.

article_title: The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance
citation: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71
title: Taxonomy of grammatical and lexical cohesive devices
description: Following Halliday and Hasan (1976), the article divides cohesive devices into grammatical and lexical types. The grammatical cohesive devices are divided into four branches: "reference", "substitution", "ellipsis", and "conjunction", while the lexical cohesive devices are divided into two branches of "collocation" and "reiteration". Sanders and Maat (2006) are cited summarizing each device, e.g. reference as two linguistic elements related in what they refer to, and conjunction as an explicitly marked semantic relation. Together these devices make sentences stick together and link into larger units of paragraphs, stanzas, or chapters.
requirements: Cohesion occurs when the interpretation of some element in the discourse is dependent on that of another
target_learners: adult intermediate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: producing cohesive written discourse
examples: Participants were given writing samples with sentences that were not cohesive and coherent and asked to change them to coherent and cohesive sentences

understanding text organization
academic reading and tasks

Measured with teacher-rated SSRS and caretaker-rated RADQ

article_title: Comparing Teaching Methods of Mathematics at University Level
citation: Voskoglou, M. (2019). Comparing Teaching Methods of Mathematics at University Level. Education Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci9030204
title: Grey-number method for evaluating mean performance from linguistic grades
description: The article proposes using grey numbers (GNs), numbers with unknown position within known boundaries represented as closed real intervals, to estimate group mean performance when students are assessed with linguistic grades A–F. Each grade is assigned an interval (e.g. A∈[85,100]), and the grey representative M yields W(M) = (m1+m2)/2 as "a reliable estimation of the student group mean performance". This avoids dilemmas about exact numerical scores and reduces student anxiety, but prevents conventional statistical testing.
requirements: Linguistic (interval) grades rather than exact numerical scores
Interval arithmetic operations on grey numbers
constraints: Prevents the application of conventional statistical methods and tests
target_learners: university students assessed with linguistic grades
target_learning_goals: evaluation of student group mean performance in mathematics

article_title: The Prisoner's Dilemma and Economics 101: Do Active Learning Exercises Correlate with Student Performance?
citation: Byun, C.H.C. (2014). The Prisoner's Dilemma and economics 101: Do active learning exercises correlate with student performance? Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 14(5), 79-91. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotlv14i5.12950
title: The Grade Game: an in-class single-play Prisoner's Dilemma with exam points at stake
description: The Grade Game is a single play simultaneous move game with a dominant strategy, modeled after the classic Prisoner's Dilemma, played in Eco101 after a Game Theory module covering dominant strategies and the Nash Equilibrium. Students are randomly paired and circle MORE or LESS points on the next exam: "If one student chooses MORE while his partner chooses LESS, he will receive 2 extra points and the partner will receive -10 points." Outcomes are designated as points that can be won or lost on the next in-class exam to make the game realistic.
requirements: In-class play so the instructor can enforce the restriction of communication between students and give each student equal time to participate
constraints: Bonus or penalty points were not actually awarded on the subsequent exam; this was announced at the end of the class period
target_learners: undergraduate students in a Principles of Economics course
target_learning_goals: understanding the Prisoner's Dilemma, dominant strategies, and the Nash Equilibrium as applied to oligopolistic market structure
examples: Conducted in one Eco101 section per semester across Spring 2013, Fall 2013, and Spring 2014 at a private liberal arts college for men in Indiana, with 71 of 75 students playing

article_title: Group Dynamic Assessment of L2 Learners' Writing Abilities
citation: Karim Shabani. (2018). Group Dynamic Assessment of L2 Learners' Writing Abilities. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 6(1), 129-149. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Group dynamic assessment grounded in Vygotskian sociocultural theory
description: G-DA is a classroom-format variant of dynamic assessment that, following Lantolf and Poehner, "integrates assessment and instruction into a seamless, unified activity" sensitive to a group's current abilities. It rests on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, scaffolding, and mediation, and uses a microgenetic method to track moment-by-moment change. The teacher moves the entire class forward in its ZPD while co-constructing ZPDs with individual learners, operating through graduation, contingency, and dialogic negotiation.
requirements: A mediator who can graduate interventions, remain contingent by withdrawing scaffolding when autonomy appears, and engage in dialogic collaboration to identify learners' ZPDs
constraints: Poehner (2009) is cited as noting classroom contexts do not permit the one-on-one format of DA, making the boundaries of a group ZPD difficult to establish a priori
target_learners: L2 writing learners in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: L2 writing ability
self-regulation in writing revision
examples: The study's G-DA procedure negotiated topics, selected student essays for board-based revision, and offered prompts from most implicit to most explicit following Aljaafreh and Lantolf (1994)

title: Teach grammar through practice and activities rather than rules and memorisation
description: The article argues that grammar teaching must be based on practice rather than theoretical knowledge, because teaching only rules and vocabulary causes them to be forgotten quickly; rules should instead be selected from literary works and written texts. In its recommendations, it states that grammar is not just a set of rules and that lessons should be designed "not based on memorization", grasping language rules and building language competencies as habits through activities.
requirements: Activities and examples that move grammar as far from the abstract as possible
constraints: Recommendation framed for Turkish language grammar curriculum and teacher training
target_learners: Secondary school students learning Turkish grammar
target_learning_goals: Durable understanding of grammar rules and language competencies
examples: The article recommends handling grammar topics holistically rather than in pieces, making them non-exam based, and encouraging students to avoid memorising

title: Group time series design for single-group instructional intervention studies
description: A group time series design involves repeated pretests and posttests on a single group, allowing researchers to track development over multiple measurement points. In this study, the design included two pretests, three treatment sessions (X1-X3), and three posttests across 10 weeks with 20 teaching hours. This design helps establish whether improvement follows the intervention rather than natural maturation, by comparing pretest-to-pretest stability against pretest-to-posttest gains.

A stable measurement instrument across all test sessions
constraints: No control group, limiting causal inference

description: The article recommends that when using instructional tools like computer games in education, "educators must get h elp from learning theories and researches". citation: Mermelstein, A. D. (2015). Improving EFL learners’ writing through enhanced extensive reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 182–198. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

description: The study's reading materials consisted of two graded reader series, the Oxford Bookworms and the Penguin Readers, at levels 1–6, with "approximately 600 graded reader books available for this study, with approximately 100 books available for participants to select from at each level". article_title: Adult Hispanic ESL Students and Graded Readers
citation: Liza E. Martinez. (2017). Adult Hispanic ESL Students and Graded Readers. The CATESOL Journal, 29(2). https://www.catesol.org
title: In mixed-level ESL classes, offer graded readers so students can read at their independent level on topics that interest them
description: The article argues that because ESL classes are heterogeneous in reading level, a single course text bores advanced students while lower-intermediate students struggle. It recommends that "Reading materials such as graded readers can enable a participant to read at his level," and that students can choose topics of interest. A means of checking comprehension, such as short quizzes per book

transition to reading authentic academic texts

article_title: Graduation Coaching in a Rural District School
citation: Zeller, P. J., Carpenter, S., Lacefield, W. E., & Applegate, E. B. (2013). Graduation coaching in a rural district school. GEAR UP Learning Centers, Western Michigan University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555555
title: Graduation coaching logic model: proactive identification, individualized student plans, and data-driven monitoring within a constructivist socio-cultural framework
description: The graduation coaching logic model is a case-management-based intervention adapted from health care and social services, in which a coach "developing/monitoring/modifying an educational development plan" meets weekly with at-risk students, arranges tutoring, liaises between school and home, and monitors academic progress at least weekly. Grounded in constructivist and socio-cultural theory, coaches help students "co-construct viewpoints from which they can understand how their personal world and their educational world intersect." The model was implemented in a rural high school with data-driven classification dashboards, real-time gradebook access, and an Activity Reporting System supporting formative and summative evaluation.
requirements: A dedicated graduation coach (half-time in this study) with access to electronic gradebook and confidential student records
Cooperation from students and parental involvement and support
Referral programs and support services for individual students
constraints: Coaching is a resource and staff intensive process
Coaching may not be the right support service for all students; students not responding within a reasonable period may be removed from the caseload
Graduation coaching may not be enough to help students overcome academic problems because of the complexity of personal and behavioral problems
target_learners: at-risk 9th-grade high school students in rural settings
target_learning_goals: improve core-course academic performance
promote student retention and progression to graduation
examples: A half-time graduation coach, an experienced high school counselor, served a caseload of 35 identified at-risk 9th graders using classification dashboards, weekly meetings, and individualized Student Plans

title: Use group discussion as an approach for teaching reading comprehension in EFL contexts
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers use structured group discussion (Book Club, Literature Circles, or Instructional Conversations) instead of or alongside basal comprehension instruction to promote higher-order reading comprehension. The author states "the results of this study support the recommendation that teachers should use group discussion as an approach for practice, as it could generate considerable positive effects." Discussion-based approaches improved interpretive comprehension, theme essays, and transfer to new texts without harming factual comprehension.
requirements: Teachers need training in the discussion approach; the study provided a three-day initial training covering theory, practice, and lesson scripts.
constraints: The study notes that "the differences that favor the discussion-based approaches were far from large, they showed a consistent pattern on several measurements."
Results generalize only to students who attended class regularly, as 15 students (9% of enrollment) were excluded from analysis.

non-English-major college freshmen
target_learning_goals: higher-order reading comprehension
interpretive comprehension of literary texts
transfer of reading skills to new texts

article_title: Graphic Novels: An Alternative Approach to Teach English as a Foreign Language
citation: Öz, H., & Efecioğlu, E. (2015). Graphic novels: An alternative approach to teach English as a foreign language. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(1), 75-90. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075216
title: Use graphic novels as alternative reading materials to teach literary texts in EFL classrooms
description: The article recommends integrating graphic novels into EFL syllabi as an alternative to plain literary texts, because they appeal to students' visual senses and improve comprehension of literary devices, inference, and vocabulary. The authors state that "graphic novels should be considered as a useful material in the foreign language teaching process and thus be implemented in the syllabi of similar schools."

vocabulary
inference
