article_title: Scaffolding EFL Students' Writing through the Writing Process Approach
citation: Faraj, A. K. A. (2015). Scaffolding EFL Students’ Writing through the Writing Process Approach. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(13), 131-141. https://www.iiste.org/Journals/index.php/JEP/article/view/23823
title: Graves' five-stage writing process (prewriting, drafting, revising, editing, publishing) as the instructional structure for EFL writing.
description: The study structures EFL writing instruction around Graves' five-stage writing process, in which "students start with w riting process approach such as Prewriting, Drafting, Revising, Editing, and ended with Publishing." Each stage has defined student activities: prewriting involves choosing topics and outlining, drafting emphasizes content over mechanics, revising focuses on content and organization, editing targets mechanical errors, and publishing involves sharing finished writing with an audience. The author notes these stages are recursive rather than linear, allowing writers to move back and forth between stages.
requirements: Students take the role of writers and follow the same steps that writers apply during their writing process
constraints: The stages are recursive rather than linear, so writers may return to earlier stages before publishing
target_learners: EFL college students
target_learning_goals: improved writing ability
confidence in expressing ideas in writing
examples: Students wrote on topics based on their own experiences, gathered and organized ideas, wrote rough drafts emphasizing content, revised based on teacher feedback, edited with checklists, and published final copies shared with the teacher.

Self-evaluation, peer assessment, and teacher evaluation for feedback

title: Use GRE percentiles rather than GRE scores within a nuanced holistic review

The authors also advise committees to consider both GRE sections, since the verbal and quantitative sections predicted different outcomes.

constraints: The study analyzed only students at one biomedical graduate school who completed the PhD, with a relatively small sample; the authors caution applying recommendations to larger groups.
target_learners: doctoral applicants in biomedical sciences
target_learning_goals: predicting doctoral student success in admissions decisions
examples: The GSBS admissions committee replaced GRE score cutoffs with a whole-file holistic review in which GRE results were one factor among many.

description: This pattern contrasts two ways of tracking trainee procedural behaviour. Traditional tools such as DOPS 'condenses the entire lead fixation task under a single descriptor' and record performance on a subjective 7-point Likert-type scale, producing 'substantial intra-rater and inter-rater variability'. A PBP scoresheet instead contains detailed unambiguous metrics recording whether each step was performed per definition, and how well and safely, with errors or critical errors. The article argues this enables granular tracking and timely supervisor instruction.
requirements: Metrics with operational definitions scoreable as yes/no
Errors and critical errors flagged in the scoresheet where available
constraints: Likert-based tracking is described as leading to substantial intra-rater and inter-rater variability
target_learners: Procedural trainees (novice CIED implanters)
Supervisors and assessors of procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Reliable objective assessment of procedural performance
Specific feedback addressing performance gaps
examples: Figure 2 shows the same lead fixation performance tracked by DOPS as one descriptor versus itemised PBP metrics with error coding

article_title: The predictive value of high school grade point average to academic achievement and career satisfaction of dental graduates.
citation: Al-Asmar Ayah A., Oweis Yara, Ismail Noor H., Sabrah Alaa H. A., Abd-Raheam Islam M. (2021). The predictive value of high school grade point average to academic achievement and career satisfaction of dental graduates. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-021-01662-5
title: Grades as predictors of academic and career outcomes account
description: The article organizes its inquiry around the contested account that preadmission grades predict academic and professional outcomes. It frames the debate by noting that "Employers have argued that grades are useful predictors because they reflect intelligence, motivation, and other abilities applicable to the job" while "many academics have contended that grades are not good predictors of job performance." The study tests this account by correlating HS-GPA with graduating AA-GPA and AA-GPA with career choices and job satisfaction, finding support for the academic-prediction half but a negative link to satisfaction.
requirements: Longitudinal or retrospective records linking admission grades to later academic and career outcomes.
constraints: The article states correlations below 0.40 have limited predictive value and that retrospective designs cannot study other contributing factors such as life events and personal characteristics.
target_learners: Dental students
Recently graduated dentists
target_learning_goals: Understanding how admission grades relate to academic achievement and later career satisfaction
examples: The study matched archived HS-GPA and AA-GPA records of 736 graduates with survey responses from 333 recent graduates.

article_title: Preferred teaching styles of medical faculty: an international multi-center study.
citation: Dash Nihar Ranjan, Guraya Salman Yousuf, Al Bataineh Mohammad Tahseen, Abdalla Mohamed Elhassan, Yusoff Muhamad Saiful Bahri, Al-Qahtani Mona Faisal, van Mook Walther N. K. title: Grasha's five classic teaching styles model (expert, formal authority, demonstrator, facilitator, delegator)
description: The study's organizing framework is Grasha's model, in which "Grasha's model includes five classic teaching styles": expert (knowledgeable subject expert giving correct information), formal authority (manager emphasizing strict rules), demonstrator (role model encouraging one effective approach), facilitator (guiding by questions, options and alternatives), and delegator (concerned with students' autonomy, helping only on request). The article operationalizes these as five eight-item subscales of the 40-item Grasha-Riechmann inventory and maps expert, authority and demonstrator to teacher-centered approaches and facilitator and delegator to student-centered approaches.
requirements: Administered as a validated 40-item close-ended inventory with eight items per style category
constraints: The article notes most higher-education teachers follow a multi-modal approach, possessing elements of all five styles to varying degrees
target_learners: medical faculty teaching undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: awareness of preferred teaching styles to align instructional pedagogies with student-centered learning
examples: The inventory was administered online to 248 faculty across seven medical schools, with Cronbach's alpha reliability of 0.73-0.82 per style

article_title: How important is distractor efficiency for grading Best Answer Questions?
citation: Puthiaparampil Thomas, Rahman Mizanur. (2021). How important is distractor efficiency for grading Best Answer Questions? BMC Medical Education, 21:29. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02463-0
title: Grade Best Answer Questions for reuse using discrimination and difficulty indices together with distractor efficiency, treating 50% or higher DE as sufficient
description: The article recommends evaluating BAQ items with DIFi, DISi and DE together rather than rewarding maximal DE. Because DE did not track item quality classes and 100% DE items were not the best, the authors "suggest that 2 or more FDs per item or 50% or higher DE as optimum" when selecting items for reuse. Items in classes A, B and C were banked, D put in a remediable category and E discarded.
requirements: Item analysis producing DIFi, DISi and distractor efficiency or functional distractors per item for each question
constraints: The study could not analyse score distribution, standard error of measurement or reliability coefficients due to unavailability of some test scores
Only one of the seven tests used 4-option items, so the 4-option findings rest on a single test
target_learners: undergraduate medical students sitting final professional examinations
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable assessment of clinical knowledge via multiple-choice testing
examples: 350 BAQ items from 7 final professional examinations were sorted into five DISi-based classes; classes A, B and C were banked, D remediable and E discarded

article_title: Applying Graph Theory to Examine the Dynamics of Student Discussions in Small-Group Learning.
citation: Chai A., Le J. P., Lee A. S., Lo S. M. (2019). Applying Graph Theory to Examine the Dynamics of Student Discussions in Small-Group Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education 18(2):ar29. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-11-0222
title: Graph theory talk-turn methodology for quantifying small-group discussion dynamics
description: The article adapts graph theory, modeling group participants as nodes and defining a talk-turn edge when "one participant talks after another." Directed, weighted edges track the sequential order and frequency of talk-turns, and parameters (degree, density, degree centrality, centralization, subgraphs) quantify individual participation and group-level dominance. The authors position this as a quantitative complement to discourse analysis, developed through three data-collection iterations and two refinements of the calculations.
requirements: Recording of ordered talk-turn data (question-or-response format) for each participant in the group
constraints: The methodology tracks only the sequential order of talk-turns and not the content of discussion
It does not consider whether an individual is addressing the entire group or a specific person
target_learners: introductory biology undergraduate students in peer-led small groups
target_learning_goals: understanding and assessing how students participate and engage in group discussions
examples: Three case studies: a decentralized group (density 1.00), a centralized group (centralization 1.00), and an eight-person group with two gender-divided subgroups

title: GRADYS game: a VR-based cognitive training game with attention, memory, language and visuospatial modules
description: The GRADYS game is a VR-based cognitive training containing four modules: attention, memory, language, and visuospatial processing, with task scenarios "inspired by daily life" and three difficulty levels per module. It was controlled with the Oculus Rift DK2 and the Xbox 6DOF control pad and included a tutorial module for learning the interface. In the study, participants completed eight individual sessions, two per week, each pairing two modules, with difficulty advancing at 75% accuracy and dropping below 50% accuracy, accompanied by a training assistant.
requirements: A training assistant accompanied participants throughout the whole session
A tutorial module to help participants learn the game interface
Difficulty progression rules: advance at 75% accuracy, return to a lower level below 50% accuracy
constraints: Controlled with the Oculus Rift DK2 and the Xbox 6DOF control pad, which the authors state made control difficult for participants with mild dementia
The authors state use in persons living with dementia would require several hardware and software modifications

visuospatial processing

article_title: Do changing medical admissions practices in the UK impact on who is admitted? An interrupted time series analysis.
citation: Fielding Shona, Tiffin Paul Alexander, Greatrix Rachel, Lee Amanda J, Patterson Fiona, Nicholson Sandra, Cleland Jennifer. (2018). Do changing medical admissions practices in the UK impact on who is admitted? An interrupted time series analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-023274
title: Medical schools should collect and scrutinise their own admissions data at a granular level to establish baselines and evaluate the impact of selection changes
description: The article recommends that schools monitor their own admissions data at a fine-grained level, as done in its case studies, because aggregate data cannot reveal whether selection changes affect who is admitted. The authors "urge schools to collect and scrutinise their own data at a granular level, akin to the approach taken in our case studies", so a baseline exists and any policy change can be evaluated. This follows from their finding that within-school variation made little discernible difference to admissions diversity.
requirements: Schools must have access to granular, linked admissions and demographic data over sufficient years before and after a policy change
constraints: The article notes its data were held in a safehaven and not publicly available, and that school-level presentation was restricted to preserve anonymity
target_learners: medical school applicants
medical school admissions staff
target_learning_goals: widening access and increasing diversity of medical school intakes
examples: Four case study schools were analysed individually with segmented regression around their largest selection policy amendment, using pre- and post-interruption admission proportions

article_title: Does the acceptance of hybrid learning affect learning approaches in France?
citation: Marco Lionel Di, Venot Alain, Gillois Pierre. (2017). Does the acceptance of hybrid learning affect learning approaches in France?. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2017.14.24
title: Grenoble-Alpes 4-step flipped-classroom hybrid learning method with a local LMS
description: A hybrid learning model used in health studies at Grenoble-Alpes University since 2006, in which "A 4-step learning method was proposed for students": remotely-accessible knowledge capsules, interactive online questions for the lecturer, interactive on-site training and explanation meetings, and participation in training-exam sessions or practice tests with junior tutors. Each theme is split across 4 sequential weeks, and the method is supported by a local LMS offering learning activities and a planner that schedules and provides access to activities at specific times.
requirements: A local learning management system providing access to learning activities and a planner scheduling activities at specific times
constraints: Not all lectures are flipped in later years, so time management is needed to manage both types of lectures; the study's learning situation is described as not generally reproducible

second-year midwifery, medical, and pharmacy students

preparation for competitive examinations and professional practice

article_title: Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter.
citation: Theobald EJ, Eddy SL, Grunspan DZ, Wiggins BL, Crowe AJ. (2017). Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181336
title: Perceived group dynamics (domination, comfort, friendship) mediate the relationship between group-work structure and individual content mastery
description: This article frames small-group learning outcomes as depending on how students perceive group dynamics, measured with three validated survey items: whether a friend was in the group, whether a group member dominated discussion, and whether the student felt comfortable. In this account, dysfunctional groups dominated by one individual depress individual content mastery, while comfort supports it; activity structure shapes these perceptions, with a jigsaw designed for positive interdependence reducing dominator reports. The framework treats equity in participation as central to who benefits from collaborative learning.
requirements: Measuring group dynamics requires validated student self-report items administered in conjunction with group activities and matched content pre-/post-tests
constraints: The study used repeated measures within one introductory biology course at a single large R1 university, with topics limited to three biology units
Demographic groups were aggregated for statistical power, and students were not randomly assigned to sections
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biology, primarily second-year students
target_learning_goals: understanding how group dynamics relate to individual content mastery in active-learning classrooms
examples: Surveys were administered three times during the quarter after intentionally constructed group activities, using items such as 'One group member dominated discussion during today's group activity' on a 6-point Likert scale.
key_sources: Theobald EJ, Eddy SL, Grunspan DZ, Wiggins BL, Crowe AJ. (2017). Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181336
